```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4, dpi = 90)
library(varm)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
fit <- varm(yraw, p = 2)
```

## 1. The identification problem

The reduced-form VAR delivers innovations $u_t$ with covariance $\Sigma$. A
structural VAR posits $u_t=P\varepsilon_t$ with orthonormal shocks,
$E[\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t']=I_K$, which requires $PP'=\Sigma$. Any such $P$
can be written $P=\tilde P Q$ where $\tilde P=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)$ and $Q$ is
an orthogonal matrix ($QQ'=I$). The data pin down $\Sigma$, hence $\tilde P$,
but say nothing about $Q$: there are $K(K-1)/2$ free parameters, and different
$Q$ give observationally equivalent models with different impulse responses
$\Theta_h=\Phi_h P$. An *identification scheme* is a set of assumptions that
selects $Q$ (point identification) or restricts it to a set (set
identification). Each `id_*()` constructor in `varm` returns such a scheme and
is passed as the `id` argument of `irf()`, `fevd()` and `hd()`, for both `varm`
(frequentist) and `bvarm` (Bayesian) fits. Results are drawn with `autoplot()`
(ggplot2) and tabulated with `tidy()`, whose columns are `response`, `shock`,
`horizon`, `estimate` and, when bands exist, `level`, `conf.low`, `conf.high`.

| constructor | assumption | identification |
|---|---|---|
| `id_chol(order)` | recursive: $P$ lower triangular after ordering | point |
| `id_longrun()` | long-run multiplier lower triangular (Blanchard-Quah) | point |
| `id_restrictions(impact, longrun)` | arbitrary zero pattern on $P$ and/or $\Theta(1)$ (A-B / mixed) | point (just-identified) |
| `id_sign(restrictions, ...)` | signs of IRFs over some horizons | set |
| `id_zerosign(sign, zero, zero_lr, ...)` | zeros and signs (ARRW) | set (weights not implemented) |
| `id_proxy(z, fit)` / `proxy_draws()` | external instrument for one shock | point, one shock |
| `id_hetero(fit, regime)` | two variance regimes (Rigobon) | point, statistical shocks |
| `id_given(P)` | user supplied impact matrix | point |

### 1.1 The A/B model, counting and observational equivalence

The general structural form (Amisano and Giannini, 1997; Luetkepohl, 2005, ch. 9) is
$$
A\,u_t = B\,\varepsilon_t,\qquad \varepsilon_t\sim(0,I_K),
$$
so that $\Sigma = A^{-1}BB'A^{-1\prime}$ and the impact matrix is $P=A^{-1}B$.
Three special cases cover most practice: the *A-model* ($B=I$, so $Au_t=\varepsilon_t$, structural
shocks with unit variance after normalising the diagonal of $A$), the
*B-model* ($A=I$, $u_t=B\varepsilon_t$, which is the form used by `varm`) and the
*AB-model*. $\Sigma$ has $K(K+1)/2$ distinct elements, while $P$ has $K^2$, so
a **necessary order condition** is that the restrictions supply at least
$$
K^2-\frac{K(K+1)}{2}=\frac{K(K-1)}{2}
$$
independent restrictions. For $K=3$ that is three. The condition is not sufficient
(Rubio-Ramirez, Waggoner and Zha, 2010 give the exact rank condition for zeros):
$P$ is identified up to the sign of each column, i.e. up to the $2^K$ matrices $PD$ with
$D$ diagonal $\pm1$. This sign indeterminacy is resolved by a *normalisation*, which is a
convention and not an identifying assumption, but it changes what "a positive shock" means.

**Observational equivalence.** If $P$ and $\tilde P=PQ$ with $QQ'=I$ both satisfy $PP'=\Sigma$, the
likelihood, the forecasts and the reduced-form IRFs coincide; only the structural
IRFs $\Phi_hP$ and the labels of the shocks differ. Identification restrictions are
therefore *untestable* in the just-identified case, and only over-identifying restrictions leave
a testable implication. In `varm`, over-identification is rejected by `id_restrictions()`.

```{r rotation-demo}
Pc <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))                              # one admissible P
th <- 0.7; Q <- matrix(c(cos(th), sin(th), 0, -sin(th), cos(th), 0, 0, 0, 1), 3)   # a rotation in the (1,2) plane
Pq <- Pc %*% Q
c(`PP' = Sigma for chol` = max(abs(Pc %*% t(Pc) - fit$Sigma)),
  `PP' = Sigma for rotated` = max(abs(Pq %*% t(Pq) - fit$Sigma)))
round(cbind(chol_col1 = Pc[, 1], rotated_col1 = Pq[, 1]), 3)   # same fit, different "first shock"
```

Both matrices reproduce $\Sigma$ to machine precision, yet they imply different first shocks.
Everything that follows is a way of choosing $Q$ (equivalently, $P$).

## 2. Cholesky (recursive) identification

**Definition.** Order the variables $(y_1,\dots,y_K)$. Take
$P=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)$ (lower triangular, positive diagonal). Then shock $j$
affects variables $j,\dots,K$ on impact but not variables $1,\dots,j-1$:
variable $i$ responds *contemporaneously* only to shocks $1,\dots,i$. The
restriction is $K(K-1)/2$ zeros in $P$, which exactly identifies the model.

**Economic story (monetary policy).** Order `infl`, `unemp`,
`rate` (the column order of `yraw`). The assumption is that prices and unemployment are predetermined within
the quarter with respect to monetary policy (they are sticky and do not react to
a policy surprise in the same quarter), while the central bank sets the rate
after seeing current inflation and unemployment. The last shock is then the
monetary-policy shock. This is the classic recursive scheme of Christiano,
Eichenbaum and Evans (1999).

```{r chol}
ir1 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 20, ci = "wild", nboot = 300)
round(ir1$estimate[, , 1], 3)   # impact matrix P (rows: response, columns: shock): lower triangular
```

```{r chol-plot}
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate)
```

A one-standard-deviation policy shock raises the rate by about 0.7 percentage
points on impact. The path of inflation after the shock is the usual
diagnostic: a significantly *positive* response (the "price puzzle") signals
that the recursive scheme or the information set is misspecified: the VAR does
not contain what the central bank knows (for instance commodity prices or
forecasts) and the "shock" is partly an anticipated reaction to inflation.

**Ordering matters.** Only the variable ordering, not the choice of recursive
$P$ given an ordering, is a modelling decision. Moving `rate` first says the
policy rate is exogenous within the quarter, which is not a monetary-policy
shock at all. Comparing orderings is a cheap robustness check:

```{r order, fig.height = 3.4}
ir2 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = c(rate, infl, unemp)), horizon = 20, ci = "none")
round(ir2$estimate[, "rate", 1], 3)   # impact responses to the "rate" shock when rate is ordered first
# ribbon and solid line: rate last; dashed: rate first
autoplot(ir1, shocks = rate) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir2), shock == "rate"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")
```

The residual correlation (`cor(resid(fit))`) tells you how much the ordering can
matter: with correlations near zero all orderings agree. Here the rate and
unemployment residuals have a correlation of about $-0.35$, so the order
matters for those two.

**All orderings.** With $K=3$ there are six orderings. The response of inflation at $h=4$ to the
shock attached to the policy rate (the shock labelled `rate` in the output, whichever position it takes in the recursion) shows
how much the answer depends on the assumption:

```{r order-all}
nm <- colnames(yraw)
perms <- list(c(1, 2, 3), c(1, 3, 2), c(2, 1, 3), c(2, 3, 1), c(3, 1, 2), c(3, 2, 1))
tab <- t(sapply(perms, function(o) {
  e <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = all_of(nm[o])), horizon = 4, ci = "none")$estimate
  c(rate_shock_on_inflation_h4 = e["infl", "rate", 5], rate_shock_on_rate_h0 = e["rate", "rate", 1])
}))
rownames(tab) <- sapply(perms, function(o) paste(substr(nm[o], 1, 3), collapse = ">"))
round(tab, 3)
```

Only orderings that put `rate` *last* give the policy-shock interpretation of section 2; the others show
the range of what other timing assumptions would imply. Cholesky orderings are observationally equivalent in fit, so the data cannot choose
among them.

### Normalisation: one standard deviation vs unit shocks

With $PP'=\Sigma$ shocks have unit variance, so responses are to a
one-standard-deviation shock. Policy discussions usually want a fixed size
shock, such as 25 basis points. `irf(normalise = normalise_to(shock, variable, size))`
rescales the shock so that the impact response of `variable` equals `size`
(draw by draw, so the bands reflect the rescaling too).

```{r norm}
irn <- irf(fit, horizon = 20, ci = "wild", nboot = 300,
           normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 0.25))
round(irn$estimate["rate", "rate", 1], 3)           # impact response is exactly 0.25
round(irn$estimate[, "rate", c(1, 5, 9, 13)], 3)
```

The normalisation changes only the *scale* of the responses for point
identified schemes (all of them scale linearly), but for ratios
across variables it avoids a classic pitfall: comparing responses in
"standard-deviation units" across models whose shock variances differ.

## 3. Long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah)

**Definition.** Let $F=I-\sum_l A_l$. The long-run (cumulative) multiplier of
the structural shocks is
$$
\Theta(1)=\sum_{h=0}^\infty \Theta_h=F^{-1}P .
$$
Blanchard and Quah (1989) impose that $\Theta(1)$ is lower triangular: shock
$j$ has no permanent effect on variables $1,\dots,j-1$. `varm` computes
$\Theta(1)\Theta(1)'=F^{-1}\Sigma F^{-1\prime}$, takes its Cholesky factor
$L$, and sets $P=FL$. The order of the variables is the column order of the data.

**Economic story (supply and demand).** In the original application
$y_t=(\Delta \text{GDP}_t,\ \text{unemployment}_t)'$, the first shock is
"supply" (the only shock with a permanent effect on output) and the second is
"demand" (transitory by assumption). Variables must be stationary (growth rates
or differences) for the long-run matrix to be meaningful. `yraw` has no output series, so we illustrate the
mechanics with $y_t=(\Delta \pi_t,\ u_t)'$: the first shock is the only one
that can permanently change the level of inflation (a "nominal trend" shock) and
the second is transitory for inflation.

```{r longrun}
d2 <- data.frame(dinfl = diff(yraw$infl), unemp = yraw$unemp[-1])
f2 <- varm(d2, p = 2)
round(max(stability(f2)), 3)
ir_lr <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 300, ci = "none")
round(apply(ir_lr$estimate, c(1, 2), sum), 3)    # cumulated long-run matrix: upper-right entry is 0
```

**Cumulative responses.** The IRF of a differenced variable is the response of
its *growth rate*; the response of its *level* is the running sum.
`cumulative = dinfl` cumulates that variable's response over the horizon, for
each draw, before bands are computed:

```{r cum, fig.height = 3.4}
ir_c <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 40, ci = "wild", nboot = 300, cumulative = dinfl)
autoplot(ir_c, responses = dinfl)   # level of inflation after the permanent (first) and the transitory shock
```

The level of inflation converges to a non-zero value after shock 1 (the long-run
effect by construction) and returns to zero after shock 2 (restricted to
zero, so the bands pinch near zero at long horizons).

**I(1) caveats and weak-instrument-like behaviour.** If the variables are I(1) and cointegrated, $F=I-\sum A_l$ is
singular and $F^{-1}$ does not exist: model the cointegrating relations (not possible in this package) or difference the
variables, accepting that over-differencing a stationary variable (or a cointegrated pair) corrupts the long-run
restriction. With a VAR in levels of a near-integrated system $F$ is nearly singular, so tiny errors in $\hat A_l$
are amplified in $F^{-1}$: the long-run multiplier behaves like a ratio with a near-zero denominator, as for a weak
instrument. A small simulation (bivariate, true $\Theta(1)$ lower triangular with long-run effect $0.5$ of shock 1 on variable 2)
shows the spread of the estimate rising with persistence $\rho$:

```{r bq-mc}
set.seed(5)
bq_one <- function(rho, n = 200) {
  Fm <- (1 - rho) * diag(2); L <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0, 1), 2); Pm <- Fm %*% L      # Theta(1) = L, lower triangular
  y <- matrix(0, n + 50, 2); for (t in 2:(n + 50)) y[t, ] <- rho * y[t - 1, ] + Pm %*% rnorm(2)
  f <- varm(y[-(1:50), ], p = 1)
  sum(irf(f, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 150, ci = "none")$estimate[2, 1, ])     # estimated long-run effect
}
sapply(c(`rho=0.5` = 0.5, `rho=0.9` = 0.9, `rho=0.97` = 0.97), function(r) { x <- replicate(100, bq_one(r)); c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)) })
```

The true value is $0.5$. The standard deviation grows markedly as $\rho\to1$ (and the estimate acquires finite-sample bias),
which is the Faust-Leeper (1997) and Christiano-Eichenbaum-Vigfusson (2006) warning in numbers.

**Pitfalls.**

* The restriction is on the *long-run* multiplier $F^{-1}$, which is poorly estimated when the VAR is near-integrated
  (Faust and Leeper, 1997; Christiano, Eichenbaum and Vigfusson, 2006): small errors in
  $\sum_l A_l$ become large errors in $F^{-1}$. Check bands; use bias
  correction (`bias_correct = TRUE`) or a Bayesian VAR.
* Whether a variable is modelled in levels or differences changes the
  identification: over-differencing a stationary variable distorts the restriction.
* The sign of each column is fixed by the Cholesky factor (positive long-run
  diagonal), not by economics. Flip signs if you want a "positive supply shock".

## 4. Sign restrictions

**Definition.** Sign restrictions (Faust, 1998; Canova and De Nicolo, 2002;
Uhlig, 2005) use $S_{ij}(h)\in\{-1,0,+1\}$ and require the IRF of variable $i$
to shock $j$ to have sign $S_{ij}(h)$ for $h=0,\dots,H_s$. Zero entries mean
unrestricted. The *identified set* is
$$
\mathcal{Q}(B,\Sigma)=\Big\{Q:\ QQ'=I,\ \ \mathrm{sign}\big(e_i'\Phi_h\tilde P Q e_j\big)=S_{ij}(h)\ \text{for all restricted }(i,j,h)\Big\} .
$$
The algorithm of Rubio-Ramírez, Waggoner and Zha (2010) draws $Q$ from the
Haar (uniform) distribution on the orthogonal group, using the QR decomposition
of a Gaussian matrix, and keeps the draw if every column satisfies the restrictions
(column sign flips are allowed). For each reduced-form draw, `nrot` accepted
rotations are retained after up to `maxtry` attempts.
In the returned objects the shock dimension is labelled with the variable names whatever the scheme,
so with `id_sign()` index shocks by column position (below: 1 = mp, 2 = demand, 3 = supply).
The restrictions are a $K\times K$ matrix (rows: variables, columns: shocks)
imposed over `horizon` periods, or a $K\times K\times H$ array. Exact zero
*restrictions* on IRFs (as opposed to unrestricted entries) are not available in
`id_sign()`; combine them with signs in `id_zerosign()` (section 8).

**Economic story.** Three shocks distinguished by textbook New-Keynesian signs:

| shock | inflation | unemployment | interest rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| monetary-policy | $-$ | unrestricted | $+$ |
| demand | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| supply | $+$ | $+$ | unrestricted |

Each is imposed for the first four quarters (impact plus three). The restrictions
separate demand from supply by the comovement of inflation and unemployment
(a Phillips-curve sign) and the policy shock from demand by the response of
inflation. Leaving the unemployment response to monetary policy unrestricted
is the Uhlig (2005) "agnostic" approach: the response one most wants to
learn about is not imposed.

```{r sign-spec}
S <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(colnames(yraw), c("mp", "demand", "supply")))
S["infl", ]  <- c(-1, 1, 1)
S["unemp", ] <- c(0, -1, 1)
S["rate", ]  <- c(1, 1, 0)
S
id_s <- id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 1, maxtry = 5000)
```

### Two sources of uncertainty

A set-identified model has two kinds of uncertainty that frequentist or
Bayesian bands mix together:

1. **Estimation uncertainty** about $(B,\Sigma)$: the usual sampling or posterior variation.
2. **Identification uncertainty** about $Q$ within $\mathcal Q$: the data cannot say, even in an infinite sample.

Pointwise percentile bands over rotations *and* reduced-form draws combine
them, so wide bands cannot be read as "the data are uninformative": part of the
width is a consequence of the researcher's choice to leave $Q$ unrestricted
within $\mathcal Q$. Using many rotations at the point estimate isolates
identification uncertainty:

```{r sign-bands, fig.height = 3.6}
# (a) identification uncertainty only: one reduced-form point, many rotations
ir_set <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 500, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
# (b) estimation uncertainty with one rotation per bootstrap draw (mixes both)
ir_mix <- irf(fit, id = id_s, horizon = 16, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 500)
c(accept_rate_point = ir_set$accept_rate, accept_rate_boot = ir_mix$accept_rate)
dim(ir_set$draws)    # [response, shock, horizon, accepted rotations]
w <- function(ir, h) {                       # width of the 90% band, unemp response to shock 1 (mp)
  d <- subset(tidy(ir), response == "unemp" & shock == "infl" & level == 0.9 & horizon == h)
  d$conf.high - d$conf.low
}
round(rbind(`rotations only (at point estimate)` = sapply(c(0, 4, 8), w, ir = ir_set),
            `bootstrap + rotations`               = sapply(c(0, 4, 8), w, ir = ir_mix)), 3)
# shock 1 (mp) is labelled "infl" in the output: shocks carry the variable names
autoplot(ir_mix, shocks = 1) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir_set), shock == "infl"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")
```

With a sample of 213 quarters and three variables, the width of the 90% band is
almost entirely identification uncertainty: rotating at the point estimate
gives bands about as wide as the full bootstrap (the two rows above, for horizons 0, 4 and 8). More data
would shrink the second source of uncertainty but not the first.

The solid line and shaded bands are the bootstrap-plus-rotation result; the
dashed line is the median of the rotations at the point estimate.

### The median is not a model: Fry-Pagan

Pointwise medians across accepted rotations combine IRFs from different
rotations $Q^{(n)}$: the median response of unemployment to the "mp" shock may
come from one $Q$ and the median response of inflation from another, so the
median path is not the IRF of any single structural model, and responses to
different shocks need not be orthogonal. Fry and Pagan (2011) propose the single
draw whose IRFs (all variables, shocks and horizons, standardised) are closest to
the pointwise median. `irf_fry_pagan()` extracts the median-target
(MT) rotation from the accepted IRFs stored in `draws`:

```{r fry-pagan, fig.height = 3.6}
mt <- irf_fry_pagan(ir_set)$irf                      # [response, shock, horizon] of the MT draw
mt <- data.frame(subset(tidy(ir_set, bands = FALSE), shock == "infl")[c("response", "horizon")],
                 estimate = as.vector(mt[, 1, ]))
ggplot(subset(tidy(ir_set), shock == "infl" & level == 0.9), aes(horizon, estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(aes(y = conf.low), linetype = "dotted", colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = conf.high), linetype = "dotted", colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = mt, colour = varm_palette(2)[2], linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to the mp shock") + theme_varm()
```

The orange line is a coherent structural model; the blue line (pointwise median)
and the dotted 90% limits summarise the set. Report the MT model when you need
one consistent decomposition (a historical decomposition or a counterfactual).
`hd()` with `id_sign()` uses the *first* accepted rotation at the point
estimate, not the MT rotation, so treat a historical decomposition from a sign
identified model as an illustration of one admissible model.

**Pitfalls.**

* The prior over $Q$ is *not* uninformative about the IRFs: a uniform Haar prior
  on rotations implies informative priors on the impulse responses
  (Baumeister and Hamilton, 2015). With few binding restrictions the posterior
  is largely the prior.
* `accept_rate` below a few percent signals that the restrictions are
  essentially in tension with the data (or too many). A zero acceptance
  rate stops `irf()` with an error.
* Restrictions that hold for many horizons are more informative; impact-only
  restrictions are the weakest.
* The identification is only as good as the cross-shock restrictions:
  without a sign pattern that separates the shocks from each other, the
  identified shocks are not uniquely labelled.

## 5. User-supplied impact matrix

`id_given(P)` accepts any matrix; it does not check $PP'=\Sigma$. Use it to
reproduce a published impact matrix, or to feed a rotation computed elsewhere
(for example from an external routine for zero and sign restrictions).

```{r given}
P <- t(chol(fit$Sigma))
ir_g <- irf(fit, id = id_given(P), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
all.equal(unname(ir_g$estimate[, , 1]), unname(P))
```

## 6. Choosing a scheme and checking it

| question | cheap check |
|---|---|
| Is the Cholesky order innocuous? | `cor(resid(fit))`; re-run with another `order`; overlay a second `tidy()` on `autoplot()` |
| Is there a price puzzle? | Sign of the inflation response to the policy shock in the first year |
| Is the long-run restriction credible? | Width of bands at long horizons; compare to `bias_correct = TRUE` |
| Do sign restrictions bind? | `accept_rate`; compare the identified-set width to the bootstrap width |
| Is an FEVD interpretable? | `fevd()` shares are only as good as the identification |

## 7. Zero patterns on impact and long-run responses: `id_restrictions()`

`id_chol()` and `id_longrun()` are two special zero patterns. `id_restrictions(impact, longrun)`
accepts any $K\times K$ matrices with `0` where the impact matrix $P$ (or the long-run matrix
$\Theta(1)=F^{-1}P$) is restricted to zero and `NA` where it is free. Writing the zeros as
$Z_j$ for column $j$, the shocks are processed in decreasing order of the number of zeros; the
$j$-th column $q_j$ of the orthogonal matrix $Q$ is the unit vector in the null space of
$[Z_jL;\,q_1';\dots;q_{j-1}']$ ($L=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)$), which exists when the
zero counts are $K-1,K-2,\dots,0$ (just-identified). Over-identified patterns are rejected.
Each shock is oriented deterministically: the impact response of variable $j$ to shock $j$ is
positive (or, if that entry is restricted to zero, the first free entry of the column).

Two consistency checks: the lower-triangular pattern reproduces `id_chol()`, and a
lower-triangular long-run pattern reproduces `id_longrun()`.

```{r restr-check}
low <- matrix(NA, 3, 3); low[upper.tri(low)] <- 0
r1 <- irf(fit, id = id_restrictions(impact = low), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
r0 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
max(abs(r1$estimate - r0$estimate))                     # same model
lo2 <- matrix(NA, 2, 2); lo2[1, 2] <- 0
r2 <- irf(f2, id = id_restrictions(longrun = lo2), horizon = 100, ci = "none")
max(abs(r2$estimate - irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 100, ci = "none")$estimate))
```

Mixed schemes are where it earns its keep. A *non-recursive* example: in the three-variable
system suppose shock 3 moves only the rate on impact (two zeros) and shock 2 does not move the rate
(one zero), with shock 1 unrestricted. This is not a permutation of a Cholesky scheme, because
variables 1 and 2 respond to each other contemporaneously.

```{r restr-mixed}
imp <- matrix(c(NA, NA, NA,   NA, NA, 0,   0, 0, NA), 3, dimnames = list(colnames(yraw), paste0("shock", 1:3)))
imp
ir_ab <- irf(fit, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 8, ci = "none")
round(ir_ab$estimate[, , 1], 3)                         # zeros hold to machine precision
```

**Pitfall.** Zero restrictions are *not testable* when the model is just-identified, and an
impact zero is a strong claim: it asserts no response within the period. With quarterly data,
"no contemporaneous response" is a much stronger assumption than with monthly data.

## 8. Zero and sign restrictions: `id_zerosign()` (ARRW)

Pure sign restrictions leave $Q$ in a large set. Theory often supplies a few *exact*
zeros as well (Arias, Rubio-Ramirez and Waggoner, 2018: ARRW). A zero restriction on the response of variable $i$ to
shock $j$ at horizon $h$ reads $e_i'\Phi_h L\,q_j=0$, a linear constraint on $q_j$.

**Algorithm (`id_zerosign()`, following ARRW Algorithm 2).**

1. Draw a reduced-form $(B,\Sigma)$ (bootstrap or posterior); set $L=\mathrm{chol}(\Sigma)$.
2. Order shocks by decreasing number of zeros $z_j$ (feasible iff $z_{(j)}\le K-j$).
3. For $j=1,\dots,K$: let $N_j=[Z_jL;\,q_1';\dots;q_{j-1}']$; draw $q_j$ uniformly on the unit sphere of the null space of $N_j$ (a Gaussian vector projected on the null space, then normalised).
4. Form $P=LQ$, flip the sign of each column if needed, and keep the draw if all sign restrictions hold. Repeat until `nrot` rotations are accepted or `maxtry` is hit.

Zeros hold exactly by construction and $PP'=\Sigma$.

**Honest caveat: importance weights are not implemented.** ARRW show that the draws from this
null-space sampler are *not* uniform on the restricted set, and correct them with a Jacobian
weight (a ratio of determinants of $A_0$ and of the volume elements $V_i$). `varm` does not compute these weights, so accepted
draws are unweighted. The output is exact only (i) when there are no zero restrictions (then the sampler is `id_sign()`), or
(ii) when the zeros pin the rotation down up to column signs (then the weights are constant across rotations,
although they still vary over reduced-form draws). **Under partial zero
identification, treat bands as approximate** and compare with the pure-sign set.

Example. Make the monetary-policy shock (column 1, as in section 4) have zero impact effect on inflation and
unemployment (a recursive-type assumption for that one shock only) while keeping the signs for the
others. The impact sign for inflation is dropped for the policy shock since the zero replaces it.

```{r zs, fig.height = 3.6}
S3 <- array(S, c(3, 3, 4), dimnames = c(dimnames(S), list(NULL)))
S3[1, 1, 1] <- 0                                    # impact inflation response of mp: zero, not a sign
Zm <- matrix(0, 3, 3); Zm[1, 1] <- 1; Zm[2, 1] <- 1 # zero impact on inflation and unemployment, shock 1
id_zs <- id_zerosign(sign = S3, zero = Zm, nrot = 300, maxtry = 1e5)
ir_zs <- irf(fit, id = id_zs, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
ir_zs$accept_rate
round(range(ir_zs$draws[1:2, 1, 1, ]), 12)           # the two impact zeros (all accepted draws)
ir_s <- irf(fit, id = id_sign(S, horizon = 4, nrot = 300, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
# shock 1 (mp) is labelled "infl"; ribbon: zero+sign set, dashed: pure-sign median
autoplot(ir_zs, shocks = 1) +
  geom_line(data = subset(tidy(ir_s), shock == "infl"), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey20")
```

The solid line (with its ribbons) is the median of the zero-plus-sign set and the dashed line the pure-sign
median. Compare the two sets: the zeros remove the rotations that violate them. Because the zero restriction is
not conjugate, the posterior mass within this set is the approximate piece (above). For a
fully-identified zero pattern, `id_restrictions()` is exact.

Long-run zeros are available through `zero_lr` (a $K\times K$ 0/1 matrix, `1` = cumulative response is zero),
e.g. a demand shock with no long-run effect on a level; the counting rule is the same, and the same
near-unit-root pitfalls as section 3 apply.

## 9. A data-generating process with known truth

To see which methods recover the truth we need a DGP whose structural impact matrix is known. Take $K=3$,
$y_t=A_1y_{t-1}+P\varepsilon_t$ with unit-variance shocks and

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0.6&0\\-0.4&1&0\\0.5&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.1&0\\0.1&0.4&0.1\\0&0.1&0.3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The target is shock 1 (column 1 of $P$), normalised to move $y_1$ by one unit on impact. Features: (i) $P$ has $P_{12}=0.6\ne0$,
so $y_1$ responds contemporaneously to shock 2 and the recursive ordering $(y_1,y_2,y_3)$ is **wrong**; (ii) $P$ has three zeros
($P_{13},P_{23},P_{32}$) in a non-recursive pattern that `id_restrictions()` can exploit; (iii) an instrument
$z_t=\varepsilon_{1t}+\nu_t$ is available.

```{r dgp}
P0 <- matrix(c(1, -0.4, 0.5,   0.6, 1, 0,   0, 0, 1), 3)
A1 <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.1, 0,   0.1, 0.4, 0.1,   0, 0.1, 0.3), 3)
simvar <- function(n, sdv = NULL, burn = 100) {
  eps <- matrix(rnorm((n + burn) * 3), ncol = 3)
  if (!is.null(sdv)) eps[burn + seq_len(n), ] <- eps[burn + seq_len(n), ] * sdv   # sdv: n x 3 shock sd's
  y <- matrix(0, n + burn, 3)
  for (t in 2:(n + burn)) y[t, ] <- A1 %*% y[t - 1, ] + P0 %*% eps[t, ]
  list(y = `colnames<-`(y[-seq_len(burn), ], c("y1", "y2", "y3")), eps = eps[-seq_len(burn), ])
}
truth <- function(H) {                                  # response of (y1,y2,y3) to shock 1, y1 impact = 1
  Ph <- diag(3); out <- matrix(0, 3, H + 1)
  for (h in 0:H) { out[, h + 1] <- Ph %*% P0[, 1]; Ph <- A1 %*% Ph }
  out / out[1, 1]
}
set.seed(7)
sm <- simvar(400)
fs <- varm(sm$y, p = 1)
tr <- truth(12)
round(tr[, 1:4], 2)
```

Now identify shock 1 four ways, from the same sample, and compare to the truth (black).

```{r dgp-compare, fig.height = 3.6}
one <- normalise_to(y1, y1, 1)                           # impact on y1 = 1
z <- sm$eps[, 1] + rnorm(400, sd = 0.7)                  # strong instrument
Ssim <- matrix(0, 3, 3, dimnames = list(colnames(sm$y), paste0("s", 1:3))); Ssim[, 1] <- c(1, -1, 1)
ir_ch <- irf(fs, id = id_chol(), horizon = 12, ci = "none", normalise = one)
ir_ab <- irf(fs, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 12, ci = "none", normalise = one)
ir_px <- irf(fs, id = id_proxy(z, fs, target = y1, size = 1), horizon = 12, ci = "none")
ir_sg <- irf(fs, id = id_sign(Ssim, horizon = 1, nrot = 400, maxtry = 1e5), horizon = 12, ci = "none",
             normalise = one)
td_sg <- tidy(ir_sg, bands = FALSE)
td_sg$estimate <- as.vector(irf_fry_pagan(ir_sg)$irf)    # the median-target draw instead of the pointwise median
td_tr <- tidy(ir_ch, bands = FALSE)                       # same layout, filled with the truth
td_tr$estimate <- 0
td_tr$estimate[td_tr$shock == "y1"] <- as.vector(tr)      # shock-1 truth, ordered response within horizon
stacked <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(d, m) cbind(d[d$shock == "y1", ], method = m),
  list(td_tr, tidy(ir_ch, bands = FALSE), tidy(ir_ab, bands = FALSE), tidy(ir_px, bands = FALSE), td_sg),
  c("truth", "Cholesky", "restrictions", "proxy", "sign (MT)")))
stacked$method <- factor(stacked$method, c("truth", "Cholesky", "restrictions", "proxy", "sign (MT)"))
ggplot(stacked, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = method, linetype = method, linewidth = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("black", varm_palette(5)[c(5, 3, 1, 2)]), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", rep("dashed", 4)), name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(1.4, rep(0.8, 4)), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to shock 1 (impact on y1 = 1)") + theme_varm()
```

Cholesky is biased because its ordering assumption is false; the
zero-restriction scheme (which encodes the true pattern) and the proxy track the truth. The sign-identified
median target model lies within the identified set but is not guaranteed to be close: signs alone
are weak. Impact errors across one hundred samples quantify this:

```{r mc, cache = FALSE}
set.seed(11)
mc <- t(replicate(100, {
  s <- simvar(300); f <- varm(s$y, p = 1); zz <- s$eps[, 1] + rnorm(300, sd = 0.7)
  c(chol = irf(f, id = id_chol(), horizon = 1, ci = "none", normalise = one)$estimate["y2", "y1", 1],
    restr = irf(f, id = id_restrictions(impact = imp), horizon = 1, ci = "none", normalise = one)$estimate["y2", "y1", 1],
    proxy = irf(f, id = id_proxy(zz, f, target = y1), horizon = 1, ci = "none")$estimate["y2", "y1", 1])
}))
rbind(mean = colMeans(mc), sd = apply(mc, 2, sd), rmse = sqrt(colMeans((mc + 0.4)^2)))   # truth: impact of shock 1 on y2 = -0.4
```

The Cholesky mean misses $-0.4$ (a bias that does not vanish with $T$), whereas the other two are
centred on it. The proxy is the most precise here because the instrument is strong (reliability about 0.7); the
zero scheme is correct but noisier, since the three zeros identify the direction of shock 1 only through
the estimated $\Sigma$. A weak instrument would reverse the ranking (see below).

## 10. External instruments (proxy SVAR)

**Set-up.** Let $z_t$ be a scalar external instrument for shock $\varepsilon_{1t}$ and write
$u_t=s\,\varepsilon_{1t}+\dots$ with $s$ the impact vector. Mertens and Ravn (2013) and Stock and Watson (2018) require

* *relevance*: $E[z_t\varepsilon_{1t}]=\phi\ne0$;
* *exogeneity (contemporaneous)*: $E[z_t\varepsilon_{jt}]=0$ for $j>1$.

Then $\gamma=E[u_tz_t]=s\phi$, so $s\propto\gamma$, identified up to scale. `id_proxy()` estimates
$\hat\gamma=T^{-1}\sum\hat u_tz_t$ and scales it so that variable `target` moves by `size` on impact,
$s=\text{size}\cdot\hat\gamma/\hat\gamma_{target}$; the IRF is $\Phi_hs$. Only column `shock` of the IRF
array (default: the position of `target`) is identified: the other columns are zero, so **FEVD
of other shocks is meaningless**, and the FEVD of the proxy shock is only right if `size` equals the shock standard
deviation, which a proxy cannot deliver.

**Relevance.** The first stage is the regression of the `target` residual on $z_t$.
`proxy_fstat()` reports `F` (classical), `F_robust` (HC1) and `F_hac`, the Montiel Olea, Stock and Watson (2021)
Wald statistic that accounts for estimation of the VAR coefficients and serial correlation; `F_hac` is
what matters for the robust intervals. Rules of thumb: below about 10 the normalised IRF
$\hat\gamma_i/\hat\gamma_{target}$ is a ratio with a denominator near zero: it has fat tails, is not normal, and bootstrap
percentile bands undercover.

```{r proxy-f}
z_weak <- 0.08 * sm$eps[, 1] + rnorm(400)                # nearly irrelevant instrument
rbind(strong = proxy_fstat(fs, z, "y1"), weak = proxy_fstat(fs, z_weak, "y1"))
```

**Inference.** `irf(fit, id_proxy(z, fit), ci = ...)` redraws $(B,\Sigma)$ but holds $\gamma$ fixed, so it
**understates uncertainty**; use `proxy_draws()`, which carries one $\gamma^*$ per draw. It offers two bootstraps:

* `"wild"`: a common Rademacher weight $w_t$ multiplies $(\hat u_t,z_t)$. Since $w_t^2=1$,
  $T^{-1}\sum (w_t\hat u_t)(w_tz_t)=\hat\gamma$ *exactly*: the key moment is not resampled at all, and
  $\gamma^*$ varies only through the re-estimated VAR coefficients. This is why Jentsch and Lunsford (2019, 2022) show the
  wild bootstrap is invalid for proxy SVARs, with bands far too narrow.
* `"mbb"` (default): moving-block bootstrap of the pairs $(\hat u_t,z_t)$, which preserves their joint serial dependence and
  does resample the moment $\hat\gamma$; valid under strong instruments. The block length defaults to the
  Jentsch-Lunsford rule $\mathrm{round}(5.03\,T^{1/4})$, the same rule as `varm_proxy()`.

In the package's Monte Carlo (`validation/proxy-coverage.R` and `validation/ident-extra.R`, not run here) the nominal 90%
band for the impact response of a non-target variable covered the truth only 13.5% of the time with a strong instrument and
21% with a weak one (and 15% in `ident-extra.R`) under the wild
bootstrap, versus 87% for the moving-block bootstrap with a strong instrument. Band widths on one simulated sample show the same thing:

```{r proxy-boot, fig.height = 3.6}
pb_w <- proxy_draws(fs, z, nboot = 300, type = "wild", target = y1)
pb_m <- proxy_draws(fs, z, nboot = 300, type = "mbb", target = y1)
ir_w <- irf(pb_w$draws, pb_w$id, horizon = 12)
ir_m <- irf(pb_m$draws, pb_m$id, horizon = 12)
both <- rbind(cbind(tidy(ir_m), method = "mbb"), cbind(tidy(ir_w), method = "wild"))
both <- subset(both, shock == "y1" & level == 0.9)
both$width <- both$conf.high - both$conf.low
round(with(subset(both, response == "y2" & horizon %in% c(0, 2, 4)), tapply(width, list(method, horizon), c)), 3)   # 90% width, y2
subset(both, response == "y2" & horizon == 0)[c("method", "conf.low", "conf.high")]   # truth: -0.4
ggplot(both, aes(horizon, estimate, colour = method, fill = method)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = 0.2, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) + scale_fill_manual(values = varm_palette(2)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(response), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Horizon (periods)", y = "Response to shock 1 (proxy)") + theme_varm()
```

At impact, where the normalisation divides by $\hat\gamma_{target}$ and the key moment matters, the wild-bootstrap band is
roughly an order of magnitude narrower than the block-bootstrap band and here excludes the true value $-0.4$ (table and
intervals above). At later horizons the two widths are close, because the re-estimated VAR coefficients dominate. The same results are
available in one call with `varm_proxy(fit, m, method = "mbb")`, which also reports the shock series and the instrument reliability.

```{r varm-proxy}
vp <- varm_proxy(fs, m = z, target = "y1", horizon = 8, nboot = 200)
vp
round(vp$estimate[1:3, ], 3)
```

**Weak-instrument-robust sets.** `varm_proxy_robust()` implements the Montiel Olea, Stock and Watson (2021)
Anderson-Rubin-type confidence sets. For each response $\lambda$ it inverts the HAC Wald test of
$s\,e_i'\Phi_h\Gamma-\lambda\Gamma_{target}=0$; the set is one of a bounded interval, the complement of an interval,
empty, or the whole real line. With a strong instrument it is a normal-looking interval; with a weak one the honest answer is
"the data cannot tell": the set is unbounded.

```{r proxy-robust}
rb_s <- varm_proxy_robust(fs, m = z, target = "y1", horizon = 4, level = 0.90)
rb_w <- varm_proxy_robust(fs, m = z_weak, target = "y1", horizon = 4, level = 0.90)
rbind(strong = c(rb_s$lower[1, "y2", 1], rb_s$upper[1, "y2", 1], rb_s$case[1, "y2", 1]),
      weak   = c(rb_w$lower[1, "y2", 1], rb_w$upper[1, "y2", 1], rb_w$case[1, "y2", 1]))   # lower, upper, case (1 bounded, 2 complement, 4 real line)
```

(The columns are the 90% lower limit, upper limit and set type for the impact response of $y_2$; the truth is $-0.4$.)

**Pitfalls.** (i) The proxy must be uncorrelated with *all other* structural shocks, not merely
with the policy rule; high-frequency surprises can contain an information effect. (ii) If the proxy
sample is shorter than the VAR, missing values must be 0-filled only when the instrument is truly zero there; NAs are rejected. (iii) A
single instrument identifies one shock; with $r$ instruments `varm_proxy(target = c(...))` identifies $r$ shocks
up to a Cholesky-type restriction within the target block, so the order of `target` matters. (iv)
`varm_proxy_bayes()` gives a posterior alternative (see its help).

### 10.1 Full-posterior and robust-Bayes proxy-SVARs

`varm_proxy_bayes()` is limited-information: the proxy never touches $(B,\Sigma)$ and nothing restricts the shock.
Two functions add the missing machinery, both built on a [bvarm()] fit (so the reduced-form prior is
whatever you chose, e.g. Minnesota) and on a first-stage regression of the proxy,
$m_t=Dy_t+Gx_t+\sum_l H_lm_{t-l}+v_t$, with a Jeffreys prior.
Writing $\Sigma=\Sigma_{tr}\Sigma_{tr}'$ and $y_t=Bx_t+\Sigma_{tr}Q\varepsilon_t$, the proxy covariances are
$E[m_t\varepsilon_t']=D\Sigma_{tr}Q$, so exogeneity ($m$ uncorrelated with the first $K-r$ shocks) is a set of
linear restrictions on the columns of $Q$. **Convention: the `r` proxies are correlated with the last `r` shocks.**

* `varm_proxy_arw()` / `id_proxy_bayes()` (Arias, Rubio-Ramirez and Waggoner 2021 type): exact independent posterior
  draws, adding sign restrictions on the proxy shocks, a reliability truncation, and lags of $y$ and $m$ in the proxy
  equation. With one proxy the shock is point-identified; with several, exogeneity leaves an orthogonal rotation of
  the proxy shocks that only signs pin down. The draws plug into `irf()`.
* `varm_proxy_gkr()` (Giacomini, Kitagawa and Read 2022): for set-identified shocks, instead of one arbitrary prior
  on the unrevisable rotation, report the **set of posterior means** and the **robust credible region** over all priors
  on the admissible rotations (GKR Algorithm 2, with draws of $Q$ instead of a numerical optimiser).

```{r proxy-bayes-full, fig.height = 3.2}
bf <- bvarm(sm$y, p = 1, ndraw = 400, nburn = 200)
arw <- varm_proxy_arw(bf, z, target = "y1", horizon = 8)
round(rbind(truth = tr[, 1], posterior_median = arw$estimate[1, ], lo90 = arw$bands[1, , 1], hi90 = arw$bands[1, , 4]), 2)
ir_arw <- irf(bf, id_proxy_bayes(bf, z, target = "y1"), horizon = 8)   # same draws through irf()
```

The same DGP in the robust-Bayes setting. In the GKR ordering the true shock 2 ($P$'s second column,
$(0.6,1,0)'$) is one of the two non-proxy shocks, which exogeneity alone cannot tell apart. With the sign restriction
"shock 1 raises $y_1$ and $y_2$ on impact" its impact response is only set-identified:

```{r proxy-gkr}
S <- matrix(0, 3, 3); S[1:2, 1] <- 1
gk <- varm_proxy_gkr(bf, z, signs = S, shock = 1, horizon = 4, nq = 100)
rbind(set_of_means_lower = gk$lower[1, ], set_of_means_upper = gk$upper[1, ],
      robust_90_lo = gk$region[1, , 1], robust_90_hi = gk$region[1, , 4],
      single_prior_median = gk$estimate[1, ])
gk$prob_nonempty
```

The two non-proxy shocks are only identified up to a rotation in the 2-dimensional space orthogonal to the proxy
direction, so the set of means is wide, whereas the single-prior (Haar) posterior reports one narrower number that
depends on the prior. GKR recommend reporting both. The true shock 2, $(0.6, 1, 0)'$, satisfies the signs but sits at the upper edge of the identified set (it is nearly the most extreme admissible rotation), so its $y_2$ impact (1) lies slightly above the estimated set of means; the 90% robust region extends to it on $y_1$ and nearly on $y_2$. Averaging bounds over draws and approximating the set by random rotations both err on the narrow side at such boundary points.
The approximation of the identified set by random rotations
underestimates it at each draw and converges as `nq` grows; strong proxies are assumed (GKR sec. 3).

**What is not implemented.** Caldara and Herbst's (2019) Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler with a structural
measurement equation and priors on $(\beta,\sigma_\nu)$; the ARW structural-prior importance weights (volume element); and
GKR's constrained-optimiser Algorithm 1.

## 11. Identification through heteroskedasticity

If the covariance changes across two known regimes, $\Sigma_1=PP'$ and $\Sigma_2=P\Lambda P'$ with
$\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K)$ distinct, then $P$ is identified (Rigobon, 2003) up to column
order and sign, without any economic restriction. With $\Sigma_1=L_1L_1'$, take the eigendecomposition
$L_1^{-1}\Sigma_2L_1^{-\prime}=V\Lambda V'$ and set $P=L_1V$. `id_hetero(fit, regime)` implements it with shocks
ordered by decreasing $\lambda_j$ (relative variance in regime 2) and signs set so that $\mathrm{diag}(P)>0$.
It returns an `id_given()` object with the eigenvalues as attribute `lambda`.

```{r hetero}
set.seed(21)
nn <- 600; reg <- rep(0:1, each = nn / 2)
sdv <- cbind(ifelse(reg == 1, 2, 1), 1, ifelse(reg == 1, 0.5, 1))     # variance ratios 4, 1, 0.25
sh <- simvar(nn, sdv = sdv)
fh <- varm(sh$y, p = 1)
idh <- id_hetero(fh, regime = reg)
round(attr(idh, "lambda"), 2)                                          # true: 4, 1, 0.25
round(cbind(true = P0[, 1] / P0[1, 1], est = idh$P[, 1] / idh$P[1, 1]), 2)   # shock 1, y1 impact = 1
```

The estimated $\lambda$ and the first column recover the truth up to sampling error. Limits to keep in mind:

* This is a **point estimate only**: `idh` is an `id_given()` with a fixed $P$, so `irf(fit, idh, ci = "bootstrap")`
  resamples $(B,\Sigma)$ but not $P$ and understates uncertainty.
* Identification needs *distinct* $\lambda_j$; near-equal ratios mean a near-singular eigenproblem and unstable
  columns (a weak-identification problem).
* The regimes must be known (or estimated elsewhere) and $P$ constant across them.
* Shocks are statistical, ordered by volatility change; labelling them economically is a separate, untested step.

## 12. Why sign-identified bands are not like other bands, and a labelling pitfall

Sign restrictions share two pitfalls worth stating in one place.

**Shocks are indexed by position, not by name.** The shock dimension of the returned IRF array carries
the *variable* names (`colnames(yraw)`) whatever the scheme. With `id_sign()`/`id_zerosign()`/`id_restrictions()`
shock $j$ is column $j$ of the restriction matrix, so label the shocks yourself (`"mp"`, `"demand"`,
`"supply"` in section 4) and index by position. Dimnames of the restriction matrix are ignored by `irf()`.

**Bands mix model and identification uncertainty.** Pointwise percentile bands over
(reduced-form draws $\times$ rotations) combine estimation uncertainty with the *width of the identified set*.
Extra data narrows only the first. A defensible report shows both: the set at the point estimate
(many rotations, `ci = "none"`) and the full band, as in section 4, together with the Fry-Pagan model:

```{r fp-api}
fp <- irf_fry_pagan(ir_set)                     # ir_set: rotations at the point estimate (section 4)
fp$index; fp$varm_draw                          # which accepted draw; which reduced-form draw it came from
round(fp$impact, 3)                             # its impact matrix (response x shock)
```

`irf_fry_pagan()` returns a coherent structural model (an IRF array, its impact matrix, and the indexes of the draw), unlike the pointwise median,
so shocks from it can be used for historical decompositions and counterfactuals. It depends on the
prior over rotations and is a summary of the set, not an estimate.

## 13. Which identification for which question?

| shock | typical question | credible identifications in `varm` | main threat |
|---|---|---|---|
| Monetary policy | effect of a rate surprise on inflation and unemployment | `id_proxy()` with high-frequency or narrative surprises (best when an instrument exists); `id_chol()` with policy last in a rich system; `id_sign()`/`id_zerosign()` with price-puzzle-avoiding signs | information effects and weak instruments (proxy); omitted forward-looking variables (Cholesky, price puzzle); prior-driven bands (signs) |
| Fiscal | multiplier of a spending or tax change | `id_chol()` with government spending ordered first (Blanchard-Perotti-style timing, no discretionary response within the quarter); `id_proxy()` with narrative tax or spending news; `id_restrictions()` with an external elasticity in $A$ | anticipation (fiscal foresight makes the VAR non-invertible); timing assumptions at low frequency |
| Oil | effect of oil price changes on activity and inflation | `id_sign()`/`id_zerosign()` separating supply, aggregate demand and oil-specific demand by comovements; `id_proxy()` with oil-supply news; `id_chol()` with oil first | composition (the demand origin of oil price changes); sign-set width; labelled shocks are not unique |
| Technology | effect of a productivity shock on hours and output | `id_longrun()` / `id_restrictions(longrun = )` (Gali, Blanchard-Quah); `id_proxy()` with utilisation-adjusted TFP | near-unit-root persistence (poor long-run estimate), over-differencing, level vs. difference specification |
| No economic prior, volatility shifts | statistical shocks, then labelled | `id_hetero()` | weak identification, regimes must be known, point estimate only |

General guidance. (1) If you have a plausible *instrument*, prefer `id_proxy()`; it needs the weakest
assumptions about the rest of the system but gives only one shock. (2) Use signs when theory speaks
only about co-movement, and report the identified set and the Fry-Pagan model. (3) Add exact zeros
(`id_zerosign()`, `id_restrictions()`) only for things you would defend as *exact*. (4) Check robustness across
schemes: if the answer is the same under Cholesky, signs and a proxy, the identification is not doing
the work.
